sections.heading: Lossy vs Lossless: Picking the Right Compression
paragraphs: Lossy WebP uses predictive compression to discard subtle visual information that human eyes rarely notice, producing the smallest files at any given quality setting.
Lossless WebP preserves every pixel exactly but achieves smaller sizes than PNG by exploiting spatial redundancy within the image.
For photographs and complex scenes, lossy mode at quality eighty to ninety delivers an excellent balance between appearance and byte count.
For screenshots, diagrams and images with sharp text overlays, lossless mode prevents the blurry artifacts that lossy compression can introduce around high-contrast edges.

sections.heading: Measuring Real-World File Size Savings
paragraphs: A typical product photograph that weighs two hundred kilobytes as a high-quality JPG often drops to one hundred thirty kilobytes as WebP at the same perceptual quality.
Larger hero images see even more dramatic reductions, sometimes losing half their weight while remaining visually indistinguishable from the original.
These savings compound across page loads: a gallery with forty thumbnails can shave several megabytes off the initial request, noticeably improving load time on mobile networks.
Measuring the before and after sizes during conversion gives you concrete numbers to report in performance audits and stakeholder presentations.

sections.heading: Browser Compatibility and Fallback Strategies
paragraphs: Every modern browser supports WebP, including Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, making it safe for production use on contemporary websites.
Legacy browsers that do not recognize WebP can be served a JPG fallback using the HTML picture element, which lets the browser choose the best format it supports.
Content delivery networks can negotiate the format automatically, serving WebP to capable browsers and JPG to others without any change to your upload workflow.
Including both formats in your asset pipeline ensures that no visitor receives a broken image while everyone benefits from the smaller file where possible.

sections.heading: Impact on Core Web Vitals and SEO
paragraphs: Google uses Largest Contentful Paint as a ranking signal, and lighter images directly reduce the time it takes for the main visual content to render.
Cumulative Layout Shift can also improve when smaller images load faster, reducing the window during which the page layout is still settling.
Sites that consistently pass Core Web Vitals tend to rank more favorably in search results, making image format optimization a tangible SEO investment.
Tracking your performance scores before and after converting to WebP provides measurable evidence of the improvement for both technical teams and marketing stakeholders.

sections.heading: When JPG Is Still the Better Choice
paragraphs: Legacy systems that only accept JPG uploads, such as certain print services or submission portals, may not recognize WebP files.
Social media platforms that re-encode uploaded images sometimes produce better results when given a JPG source rather than WebP.
Email clients with limited image support may render WebP incorrectly, so JPG remains the safer default for newsletter graphics.
Keeping both formats in your asset library lets you choose the right one for each distribution channel based on its specific compatibility requirements.

faqs.q: What is the difference between lossy and lossless WebP?
faqs.a: Lossy WebP discards subtle visual data for smaller files, while lossless WebP preserves every pixel exactly but still achieves smaller sizes than PNG through spatial compression.

faqs.q: Will converting to WebP affect my site's SEO?
